title: The Whispering Wood: A Collector's Curse from Ambalangoda
description:
Down on Sri Lanka's southern coast, in the town of Ambalangoda, the air is thick with the scent of salty ocean and carved wood. It's a place famous for its traditional masks, used for centuries in healing rituals to ward off malevolent spirits. But some masks carry more than just history... they carry a presence.

This is the tale of Kamal Silva, a city collector who sought out a piece of authentic Sri Lankan folklore, a mask unlike any other. What he found wasn't just art, but a silent companion that would slowly unravel his life. A fictional story, steeped in the mystique of Ambalangoda's ancient traditions.
fiction_note: Based on Sri Lankan folklore surrounding ritual masks; characters and events are dramatised and fictional.

scenes.narration: What if an ancient piece of wood, carefully carved, begins to watch you back? Kamal Silva, a man of quiet tastes and a growing collection, often pondered such things. His Colombo apartment, all cool concrete and modern art, felt strangely empty without a piece of genuine Sri Lankan spirit. Not just any souvenir, mind you, but something with real power, real history. He’d heard whispers, of course, about the masks of Ambalangoda. Not the tourist pieces, but the old ones. The *real* ones. The kind that old people in the villages spoke about with a shudder, saying they held more than just painted expressions. Kamal was intrigued. He sought a mask that wasn't merely decorative, but held a secret.
visuals: Overhead shot, a modern, minimalist apartment living room at twilight, rain streaks visible on a large window overlooking Colombo city lights, a single spotlight illuminates an empty pedestal where a mask will go. 50mm lens.

A large, leather-bound book titled "Ancient Masks of Lanka" open on a glass coffee table, showing an illustration of a Sanni mask, rain blurring on the window in the background. Shallow depth of field.

scenes.narration: The tuk-tuk rattled down the wet, red-earth road, the smell of rain on hot ground thick in the humid air. Kamal had left the city’s rush behind, trading it for the southern coast’s lazy rhythm. Ambalangoda. Even the name felt heavy, ancient. He peered out, past the flapping plastic rain guard, at the small, brightly painted houses, the occasional flash of the ocean. He wasn't here for the usual tourist fare, no. He was looking for a specific kind of carving, a specific *energy*. He had heard of an old master, Perera, who kept to himself, away from the main road. The kind of carver who didn’t just chisel wood, but seemed to coax spirits from it.
visuals: A narrow, unpaved red-earth road curving through lush, rain-soaked coastal vegetation, a single yellow tuk-tuk headlight beam cutting through the misty evening, coconut trees silhouetted against a bruised sky. 35mm lens.
Close up on Kamal Silva's hand resting on the rain-streaked plastic cover of a tuk-tuk window, blurred view of green leaves and red earth beyond, drops of water clinging. Macro lens.

scenes.narration: Master Perera’s workshop was a jumble of wood shavings, half-finished masks, and the sweet, earthy scent of jak wood. Kerosene lamps cast flickering shadows, making the carved faces seem to shift and grin. Old Perera, his hands gnarled like ancient roots, looked Kamal up and down. “You’re not looking for a tourist piece, are you, young master?” he rasped, his eyes sharp. Kamal explained his desire for something authentic, something with *history*. Perera nodded slowly, a knowing look on his face. “There are masks, and then there are *masks*,” he said, his voice dropping low. “Some are best left where they belong, eh?”
visuals: Interior of a dimly lit, dusty wooden workshop at night, filled with carved masks on shelves and hanging from beams, a stoic old man in a sarong stands beside a workbench, a younger man (Kamal) stands respectfully, a single kerosene lamp casts long shadows. 28mm lens.
A gnarled hand, stained with wood dust, holds a small carving chisel, resting on a block of uncarved jak wood, blurred masks in the background.

scenes.narration: Then Perera led him to a dark corner, pulling back a heavy canvas sheet. There it was. Not painted, not polished, just raw, dark, ancient wood, almost black. It was a Sanni mask, Kamal recognized the general form, but unlike any he had seen. Its expression was not of a disease demon, but something deeper, more primordial. The eyes, unpainted, seemed to absorb the dim light. “This one… it came from the ground,” Perera murmured, tracing a finger along its brow. “Found during the temple renovations, many years ago. The old people… they said it was always there, waiting. Not for a house, sir. Not for a display.”
visuals: A dark, unpainted wooden Sanni mask (stylised, not a direct copy of a specific Sanni demon) sitting on a rough wooden shelf in a shadowed corner of the workshop, an old man’s hand (Perera) points towards it, Kamal Silva’s silhouette is partially visible, candlelight flickers. 50mm lens.
Extreme close-up on the unpainted, dark wood texture of the mask, focusing on the deep, hollowed-out eyes that seem to hold darkness, tiny dust motes visible in the faint light.

scenes.narration: Kamal felt a thrill, a shiver, but dismissed it as the excitement of a rare find. Superstition, he thought. Old wives’ tales. He saw only magnificent artistry, a piece of living history. He haggled, respectfully but firmly, for nearly an hour. Old Perera seemed reluctant to part with it, his eyes lingering on the mask as if in warning. But money spoke, and eventually, with a sigh, the old man wrapped it in coarse cloth. “Take care, young master,” Perera said, his voice grave. “Some things… they carry their own company.” Kamal smiled, thanked him, and hurried back to his waiting tuk-tuk, the rain beginning to fall harder now, drumming on the roof.
visuals: Kamal Silva, seen from behind, walking away from the dimly lit workshop into the heavy rain, carrying a wrapped bundle (the mask) under his arm, the workshop's open doorway a rectangle of flickering light behind him. 85mm lens, shallow depth of field.
Raindrops splashing on a wet, dark wooden workbench, a few scattered wood shavings, a small stack of rupee notes lying partially visible on the corner of the bench.

scenes.narration: Back in his Colombo apartment, the mask felt heavier, somehow. He unwrapped it carefully, the dark wood cool beneath his fingertips. It looked even more imposing here, against the stark white walls. He placed it on the empty pedestal he’d prepared, letting a focused spotlight illuminate its ancient, unsettling features. It was magnificent. For a few days, it was just that: a striking, powerful work of art. But soon, the quiet in his apartment began to feel… different. Not empty, but observed. The air, usually cool and dry, seemed to carry a faint, damp chill, like the coastal air he'd left behind.
visuals: A modern apartment living room at night, the dark wooden mask prominently displayed on a sleek, minimalist pedestal, a single strong spotlight creating dramatic shadows, Kamal Silva stands a few feet away, looking at it, his back to the viewer. 35mm lens.
The unpainted mask on the pedestal, shadows playing across its features from the spotlight, a faint, almost imperceptible mist or haze in the air around it, suggesting a damp chill.

scenes.narration: He blamed the old building. Or the city’s dampness. But the subtle things continued. A faint whisper, like dry leaves rustling, when there was no breeze. A fleeting shadow that darted across his peripheral vision, gone before he could focus. He'd wake up suddenly, convinced he'd heard footsteps, or the soft scrape of wood on wood. His sleep became broken, restless. He'd lie awake, staring at the ceiling, feeling an uncomfortable presence in the silent apartment. He found himself avoiding direct eye contact with the mask, his gaze always drifting away, as if it held a secret he wasn't ready to uncover.
visuals: A dimly lit apartment bedroom at night, Kamal Silva lies awake in bed, staring at the ceiling, the bedroom door slightly ajar, revealing a sliver of the living room where the mask sits, its silhouette vaguely visible. 50mm lens.
A close-up of Kamal Silva's eyes, wide open in the dark, reflecting a tiny, almost imperceptible flicker of light from an unknown source.

scenes.narration: The shifts became less subtle. He woke one morning to find the mask on its pedestal, but subtly turned, facing his bedroom door. He swore he’d left it facing the window. He moved it back, his heart thumping. The next day, it was turned again. A persistent, dull ache settled in his joints, a strange heaviness in his limbs, as if a great weight pressed down on him. He started feeling… observed. Even when he was alone, he felt eyes on his back, a cold breath on his neck. He began to feel a deep, unsettling unease, a pervasive sense of dread that clung to him like the humid air outside.
visuals: A long, dark hallway in Kamal Silva's apartment, leading to the living room, the mask on its pedestal at the end of the hallway, subtly angled towards the viewer, casting an elongated, unsettling shadow. 85mm lens.
A close-up of Kamal's hand, gripping a door frame tightly, knuckles white, his face out of frame, a sense of tension and fear.

scenes.narration: Then came the illness. A recurring fever, chills that shook him to the bone, a deep, gnawing pain in his stomach. Doctors found nothing. His energy drained away. He started to see things—fleeting figures in the shadows, glimpses of dark, dancing forms in the corner of his eye. He heard a soft, rhythmic drumming, faint but persistent, like ancient ritual music drifting from far away. Master Perera's words echoed in his mind: "Some things… they carry their own company." The mask, he realized with a chilling certainty, was not just watching him. It was *with* him. It had brought its own company.
visuals: Kamal Silva hunched over, shivering despite the heat, in a dimly lit apartment, looking frail, a blurred dark shape of the mask visible in the background, out of focus but ominous. 50mm lens.
A close-up on Kamal Silva’s ear, hearing a faint, rhythmic vibration, perhaps a blurred reflection of the mask’s eye in the background.

scenes.narration: Desperation clawed at him. He had to get rid of it. He tried to pack the mask, but his hands felt heavy, reluctant, as if an invisible force held them back. He posted it online, described it as a rare antique, but every potential buyer, after seeing a photo, would suddenly back out, citing vague "bad feelings." He even tried to give it away, discreetly, to an unsuspecting friend. But the friend, after an hour, called in a panic, saying his own house felt "wrong," and he returned it. Kamal felt a cold, crushing weight whenever he touched the mask, a feeling of absolute resistance. It was like trying to move a mountain.
visuals: Kamal Silva, appearing weary and unwell, standing in his apartment, holding a cardboard box that is clearly too large for its contents (the mask), his arms trembling slightly, a sense of struggle. 35mm lens.
A close-up of Kamal's hand, extended towards the mask (out of frame), hesitating, a visible tremor, illuminated by the cold light of a laptop screen in the background.

scenes.narration: The mask remains on its pedestal, unmoving, watching. Kamal Silva has stopped trying to fight it. He rarely leaves his apartment now, his health a constant, bewildering decline. He sits, sometimes for hours, simply staring at the dark wood, the unpainted eyes. He understands now, Perera’s warning. This wasn’t just a piece of art. It was a vessel. And it had chosen him. The rhythmic drumming, fainter now, is almost a comfort. He sometimes wonders if the others, the unseen company, are gathered around him too, silently, patiently. The air is always damp, always cold, in his apartment. Always watching.
visuals: A long shot of Kamal Silva, a frail figure, sitting alone in a darkened living room, facing the mask on its pedestal, both figures small in the frame, bathed in the dim, cold light of early dawn filtering through a window. 100mm lens.
A close-up on the unpainted mask, its dark wood features looking almost wet, a single, tiny, inexplicable bead of moisture clinging to the edge of its eye socket, catching a glint of light.

shorts.title: The Mask Collector's Deadly Bargain
shorts.narration: Down on Sri Lanka’s humid southern coast, Kamal Silva, a keen collector, found himself in a dusty, dimly lit workshop. He was searching for a mask with real history, real power. The old carver, Master Perera, showed him one unlike any other: ancient, dark wood, unpainted, its eyes seemingly alive. “This one… it came from the ground,” Perera murmured, a warning in his voice. “Not for a house, sir. Not for a display.” Kamal, a modern man, dismissed it as superstition. He saw only a magnificent piece of art. He bought it, ignoring the old man’s grave words. But some things carry their own company. And sometimes, they choose you. The full story is on our channel.
visuals: Vertical shot, dimly lit wooden workshop, old man's gnarled hands holding a dark, unpainted wooden mask, shadows cast by a single flickering kerosene lamp.
Vertical shot, close-up on the unpainted, dark wooden mask's eyes, appearing hollow and deep, with a subtle, unsettling glint.
Vertical shot, Kamal Silva (back to camera) walking out of the workshop into heavy rain, carrying a cloth-wrapped bundle, the dark doorway behind him.
Vertical shot, Kamal's modern apartment, the mask now on a sleek pedestal, dramatically lit, looking out of place yet imposing.
Vertical shot, close-up of Kamal's face, eyes wide with a subtle unease as he looks slightly past the camera, implying he feels watched.

shorts.title: What Happens When Ancient Evil Comes Home?
shorts.narration: Kamal Silva’s new antique mask from Ambalangoda was meant to be the centrepiece of his collection. But soon, the quiet in his Colombo apartment began to feel… observed. Faint whispers, fleeting shadows. He’d wake to find the mask subtly turned, its unpainted eyes now facing his bedroom door. A persistent ache settled in his joints, a strange heaviness. He began to feel truly watched, a cold breath on his neck. Then came the illness: a recurring fever, gnawing pain. Doctors found nothing. Master Perera’s warning echoed in his mind: "Some things… they carry their own company." The mask, he realized, was not just watching. It was *with* him. The full story is on our channel.
visuals: Vertical shot, the mask on its pedestal in a dark apartment, subtly turned towards the viewer, an unsettling presence.
Vertical shot, Kamal Silva lying awake in bed, staring at the ceiling, illuminated by a sliver of light from the hallway where the mask sits.
Vertical shot, close-up of Kamal's hand, trembling as he reaches for a glass of water on a bedside table, looking frail and unwell.
Vertical shot, a reflection of the mask's dark silhouette visible in a polished surface (e.g., a dark table, a window at night) in the apartment.
Vertical shot, Kamal Silva, hunched and shivering, despite the humid air, his face partially obscured, a sense of fear and desperation.
